content.text: Dreeg (a Franconian dialect form of 'Dreck', meaning trash or muck) is a complex, multiphase card game from the Nuremberg region of Germany. It is a composite game consisting of eight distinct sub-games, all based on the mechanics of Sechsundsechzig (66). Players compete to erase 'strokes' from their slate, and the game is strictly one of elimination: in each phase, players drop out as they succeed, until only one 'loser' remains to face the next challenge.

Dreeg is deeply rooted in the Franconian tavern culture of North Bavaria. It evolved as a way to extend the standard game of 66 into a longer, social competition suitable for a 'Stammtisch' (regular's table).
Ideally 4 players. Can be played by 3.
24-card German-suited deck (Bavarian or Franconian pattern). Card ranks: Ace (11), Ten (10), King (4), Ober (3), Unter (2), Nine (0).
Deck of cards, chalk slates (Schiefertafeln) for each player, chalk.
Dealer deals 6 cards to each player (in batches of 3). In some phases, a trump card is turned up; in others, trumps are determined by bidding.

items.text: Stroke notation: Some play with Roman III or a crossed seven instead of XII for the seven strokes; first stroke erased differently. Kartl-Akademie Weinzierlein uses 10 strokes (XX) per phase instead of 7.
Two-player trump indicator: In two-player 66 some use the 13th card as trump indicator under the talon; others use the bottom card of the pack turned up and slid under the talon.
Rot-Assen scoring (Bamberger): Bamberger variant: lone player always erases 3 strokes if successful in Rot-Assen, irrespective of opponents' card points; opponents still erase 1, 2 or 3 if they win.
